tagline: A mostly gravel crossing that first brought road travelers to Denali National Park.
intro: The Denali Highway climbs steeply from Paxson into the foothills of the central Alaska Range, then winds through the Amphitheater Mountains. Most of its 135 miles are gravel. Washboarding and dust are common; in good weather, the route offers views of the Alaska Range’s peaks and glaciers. The first 21 miles, reaching Tangle Lakes, are paved.

Alaska residents pressed for road access to Denali National Park in the early 1930s, after the Alaska Railroad’s construction in 1923. After World War II, the Alaska Road Commission recommended a Paxson–McKinley Park road; surveys began in 1947 and construction in 1950. The highway opened in 1957 as the park’s first road access. The original road was commissioned on August 5, 1957; a private vehicle had already traveled its length three days earlier. Primary access shifted to the Parks Highway in 1971, incorporating the Denali Highway section from Cantwell to the present park entrance.

Driving west from Tangle Lakes, the road crests at Maclaren Summit and drops into the Maclaren River valley. Beyond the Maclaren crossing it winds through Crazy Notch, follows the foot of the Denali Clearwater Mountains to the Susitna River, then crosses glacial outwash plains toward the Nenana. The final stretch follows that river down to Cantwell and the Parks Highway.

moments.title: Tangle Lakes
moments.text: Streams connect the Tangle Lakes into a 16-mile chain that forms the headwaters of the Delta River. Long, Lower, Round and Upper Tangle Lake belong to the chain. At 2,864 feet, the surrounding country is mostly tundra. Lake trout, burbot and Arctic grayling live in these waters. The lakes also lie within an extensively studied archaeological landscape: part of the area became a National Register archaeological district in 1971. Before 1976, archaeologists had discovered almost 150 sites, evidence of intermittent occupation over a much longer period than the highway’s history. Round Tangle Lake’s BLM campground and boat launch provide the main public access.

moments.title: Maclaren Summit
moments.text: Maclaren Summit puts the highway at 4,086 feet after its winding passage through the Amphitheater Mountains. The BLM’s Maclaren Summit Trail heads north from milepost 39. The highway gives road access to alpine terrain used by breeding birds, including Smith’s longspur, long-tailed jaeger and whimbrel. Across its full length, the highway passes through three principal drainage systems: the Copper River, the Tanana/Yukon and the Susitna. West of the summit, the road descends into the Maclaren River valley, with views north toward Maclaren Glacier. It crosses the river before winding onward through Crazy Notch.

moments.title: Cantwell
moments.text: Cantwell began as an Alaska Railroad flag stop supplying the Valdez Creek mining area, whose community was called Denali. Oley Nicklie, a Native Alaskan, sought railroad work after fur prices fell, and he and his two brothers founded part of the settlement. The town sits at the north end of Broad Pass, along Cantwell Creek and the Jack River, tributaries of the north-flowing Nenana. Here the Denali Highway reaches its western terminus and meets the Parks Highway. Since 1971, the Parks Highway has provided the primary road access to Denali National Park, incorporating the older highway’s stretch from Cantwell to the park entrance.

practical: Maclaren Summit: Winter travel on the highway is by snowmobile or dogsled; it is not a winter automobile route. (checked 2026-10-11)
